entries.meaning: The basic unit of money in the United States and several other countries. ---
examples: I found a dollar in the parking lot.
He makes about ninety thousand dollars a year.
The dollar gained against the euro this week.

entries.meaning: A unit of money worth one hundredth of a dollar. ---
examples: The pen cost ninety-nine cents.
I don't have a cent on me.
Every cent goes to the animal shelter.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sent and scent in American English.

entries.meaning: A flat piece of metal used as money. ---
examples: She dropped a coin in the fountain.
He keeps his coins in a jar by the door.
The machine only takes coins.

entries.meaning: The system of money used in a particular country. ---
examples: The local currency is the peso.
Several currencies fell against the dollar.
You can pay in either currency.

entries.meaning: The money returned to you after paying, or coins of small value. ---
examples: Keep the change.
Do you have change for a twenty?
I emptied the change out of my pockets.
entries.contrast: In the money sense it is uncountable — never changes.

entries.meaning: An American coin worth ten cents. ---
examples: A phone call cost a dime back then.
She counted out four dimes for the meter.
I've got a couple of dimes in my pocket.

entries.meaning: An American coin worth twenty-five cents, or a three-month business period. ---
examples: The laundry machines need quarters.
Sales were up in the third quarter.
Do you have a quarter for the parking meter?
entries.contrast: Two everyday senses: the 25-cent coin and a three-month period of a business year.

entries.meaning: An arrangement that lets you keep money at a bank. ---
examples: I opened a checking account last week.
There's nothing left in my account.
They froze both accounts during the investigation.

entries.meaning: Money put into an account, or money left as security. ---
examples: I made a deposit at the ATM.
The landlord kept our security deposit.
Direct deposits usually clear overnight.

entries.meaning: An act of taking money out of a bank account. ---
examples: There's a limit on daily withdrawals.
The withdrawal showed up on my statement.
She made a large withdrawal on Friday afternoon.

entries.meaning: The amount of money in an account, or the amount still owed. ---
examples: My account balance is down to forty dollars.
Check your balance before you spend.
They pay off their credit card balances every month.

entries.meaning: A movement of money from one account to another. ---
examples: The wire transfer takes two business days.
I set up an automatic transfer to savings.
International transfers cost extra.
entries.contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (TRANS-fer); the verb stresses the second (trans-FER).

entries.meaning: A bank employee who handles customers' cash at a counter. ---
examples: The teller asked for my ID.
Only two tellers were working.
Ask a teller to order the cash for you.

entries.meaning: A machine that lets you take cash out of your bank account. ---
examples: There's an ATM in the lobby.
Most ATMs charge a fee if you're out of network.
The ATM ate my card.

entries.meaning: A printed form ordering your bank to pay someone from your account. ---
examples: He wrote me a check for the deposit.
The check bounced.
They still mail paper checks.
entries.contrast: American spelling is check; British English writes cheque for the bank sense.

entries.meaning: A record from a bank listing the activity on an account. ---
examples: My bank statement came in the mail.
Go through the last three statements.
The charge isn't on this statement.

entries.meaning: Money paid for the use of borrowed money, or earned on savings. ---
examples: The loan carries eight percent interest.
You'll pay a lot of interest over thirty years.
The account earns almost no interest.
entries.contrast: In the money sense it is uncountable — never interests.

entries.meaning: A single act of paying, receiving or moving money. ---
examples: The transaction was declined.
You get ten free transactions a month.
Every transaction shows up in the app right away.

entries.meaning: An amount of money paid, or the act of paying it. ---
examples: The first payment is due on the first of the month.
We missed two car payments.
He set up automatic payments for the utilities.

entries.meaning: A printed proof that you paid for something. ---
examples: Keep the receipt in case you return it.
I can't find the receipt for the printer.
Save your receipts for tax season.
entries.contrast: The p is silent — say rih-SEET.

entries.meaning: A document sent to a customer listing goods or work and the amount owed. ---
examples: I'll send the invoice on Friday.
They haven't paid last month's invoice.
Three invoices are still outstanding.

entries.meaning: The ability to buy now and pay later, based on trust that you will repay. ---
examples: Her credit is excellent.
We bought the couch on credit.
They cut off his line of credit.

entries.meaning: An amount taken directly out of a bank account. ---
examples: I paid with my debit card.
The debit posted this morning.
There are two debits I don't recognize.

entries.meaning: A plastic card that lets you buy things with borrowed money. ---
examples: My credit card got declined.
He pays off his credit cards every month.
They don't take that credit card here.

entries.meaning: A number that tells lenders how reliably you repay what you borrow. ---
examples: My credit score dropped forty points.
A good credit score gets you a better rate.
Credit scores update about once a month.

entries.meaning: A sum of money borrowed that must be paid back, usually with interest. ---
examples: They took out a loan to fix the roof.
She's still paying off her student loans.
The bank approved the loan in a week.

entries.meaning: Money that one person or company owes another. ---
examples: He's finally out of debt.
They ran up huge debts on credit cards.
The company is drowning in debt.
entries.contrast: The b is silent — it rhymes with bet.

entries.meaning: A long-term loan used to buy a house, with the house as security. ---
examples: We refinanced the mortgage last spring.
Their mortgage payment eats half their income.
Mortgages got a lot more expensive this year.
entries.contrast: The t is silent — say MOR-gij, never mort-gage.

entries.meaning: A person or company that lends money. ---
examples: Shop around before you pick a lender.
The lender wanted two years of tax returns.
Several lenders turned him down.

entries.meaning: One of a series of regular payments toward a larger sum. ---
examples: You can pay in twelve monthly installments.
The last installment is due in June.
He missed an installment and they called him.
entries.contrast: American spelling doubles the l — installment; the British write instalment.

entries.meaning: Property promised to a lender in case the borrower cannot repay. ---
examples: He put up his truck as collateral.
The bank wants collateral for a loan that size.
Without collateral, the rate goes way up.

entries.meaning: A person or company that is owed money. ---
examples: His creditors have been calling all week.
The company owes three creditors over a million dollars.
A creditor can't just take your paycheck.

entries.meaning: A legal state in which someone cannot pay what they owe. ---
examples: The airline filed for bankruptcy.
Medical bills are a leading cause of bankruptcy.
Bankruptcies spiked after the crash.

entries.meaning: A failure to make payments that you are legally required to make. ---
examples: The country is close to default.
A single default wrecks your credit.
Loan defaults rose sharply last quarter.

entries.meaning: The original amount of a loan, apart from the interest on it. ---
examples: Most of the early payments go to interest, not principal.
She put an extra hundred a month toward the principal.
The principal on the loan is still forty thousand.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like principle, a rule; the money sense is spelled principal.

entries.meaning: The part of a price paid up front, with the rest borrowed. ---
examples: They're saving for a down payment on a house.
The down payment was twenty percent.
Bigger down payments mean lower monthly costs.

entries.meaning: The percentage charged for borrowing money or paid on savings. ---
examples: Interest rates went up again.
We locked in a low interest rate.
The interest rate on that card is brutal.

entries.meaning: Money put into something in the hope of earning more. ---
examples: Real estate turned out to be a smart investment.
Her investments lost value last year.
It's a long-term investment.

entries.meaning: Someone who puts money into a business or asset to earn a return. ---
examples: Investors got nervous and sold.
He was an early investor in the company.
The pitch is aimed at small investors.

entries.meaning: A share of ownership in a company that can be bought and sold. ---
examples: Tech stocks took a beating today.
She owns stock in three airlines.
He bought the stock at twelve dollars a share.

entries.meaning: The system in which company shares are bought and sold. ---
examples: The stock market closed down today.
He lost a lot of money in the stock market.
Asian stock markets opened lower.

entries.meaning: One of the equal parts a company's ownership is divided into. ---
examples: I sold half my shares in March.
Each share pays a small dividend.
They bought a hundred shares on Monday.

entries.meaning: A certificate showing that a government or company has borrowed from you. ---
examples: Government bonds pay less, but they're safe.
The city issued bonds to build the stadium.
He put the money into a ten-year bond.

entries.meaning: A share of a company's profits paid out to its shareholders. ---
examples: The company raised its dividend again.
She lives off the dividends.
That stock hasn't paid a dividend in years.

entries.meaning: Someone who owns shares in a company. ---
examples: Shareholders voted against the merger.
Every shareholder gets a proxy form in the mail.
The board answers to the shareholders.

entries.meaning: Someone who buys and sells for other people in exchange for a fee. ---
examples: Talk to a mortgage broker first.
Her broker called with a tip.
Brokers take a cut of every deal.

entries.meaning: The overall activity of buying and selling a particular thing. ---
examples: The market dropped three percent.
Emerging markets are volatile.
There's a strong market for used trucks.

entries.meaning: The value of one country's money expressed in another's. ---
examples: The exchange rate is terrible right now.
Check the exchange rate before you convert anything.
Exchange rates move all day long.

entries.meaning: Something valuable that a person or company owns. ---
examples: The court froze his assets.
Their biggest asset is the building itself.
They sold off assets to cover the debt.

entries.meaning: A debt or obligation that a person or company owes. ---
examples: The firm's liabilities exceed its assets.
That old warehouse is a liability, not an asset.
We're reviewing every liability on the books.

entries.meaning: Money available to invest in or run a business. ---
examples: They need capital to expand.
The startup raised capital from three funds.
Most of his capital is tied up in real estate.
entries.contrast: Financial capital is uncountable; a capital meaning a city is a different, countable word.

entries.meaning: The value of what you own once the debt on it is subtracted. ---
examples: We have a lot of equity in the house now.
She took a pay cut in exchange for equity.
They borrowed against their home equity.

entries.meaning: A pool of money set aside or invested for a particular purpose. ---
examples: He moved his savings into an index fund.
The scholarship fund is out of money.
Funds like this one charge low fees.
entries.contrast: In the plural, funds often just means available money — insufficient funds.

entries.meaning: The profit made on money that was invested. ---
examples: The fund posted a twelve percent return.
Returns have been flat for two years.
You won't get that kind of return without risk.

entries.meaning: The chance that an investment loses money. ---
examples: Every investment carries some risk.
He took a big risk with that money.
The risks are spelled out in the fine print.

entries.meaning: The money left over after costs are subtracted from income. ---
examples: They sold the house at a profit.
Profits were up eight percent.
The store barely turns a profit.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like prophet in American English.

entries.meaning: Money that a business or investor fails to get back. ---
examples: We sold at a loss.
The company reported losses for the third year running.
He wrote the loss off on his taxes.

entries.meaning: All the money a business takes in before costs are subtracted. ---
examples: Revenue grew ten percent last year.
Most of their revenue comes from advertising.
Ticket sales are the museum's main source of revenue.

entries.meaning: Money that a person regularly receives from work or investments. ---
examples: Their combined income is about ninety thousand.
Rent takes a third of my income.
He has no other source of income.
entries.contrast: Uncountable for one person's earnings — say a lot of income, not incomes.

entries.meaning: Money that has to be spent on something. ---
examples: Travel expenses are reimbursed.
Childcare is our biggest expense.
She submitted the expense report late.

entries.meaning: The act of using money, or the total amount used. ---
examples: Consumer spending slowed over the summer.
They cut spending across the board.
Holiday spending hit a record this year.

entries.meaning: A plan for how much money will be spent on what. ---
examples: We blew the budget on the kitchen.
The city passed its budget last night.
Both departments cut their budgets.

entries.meaning: The amount of money needed to buy, make or do something. ---
examples: The cost of living keeps going up.
Labor costs doubled in two years.
They covered the cost of the repair.

entries.meaning: The amount of money you must pay for something. ---
examples: Gas prices went up again.
What's the asking price?
He got a good price on the car.

entries.meaning: An amount charged for a service or for the right to do something. ---
examples: There's a twenty-dollar late fee.
The bank waived the fee.
Their fees are higher than everyone else's.

entries.meaning: An amount of money billed or taken for something. ---
examples: There's a charge on my card I don't recognize.
They dropped the delivery charge.
Two charges came through twice.

entries.meaning: Money the government requires people and businesses to pay. ---
examples: Property taxes went up this year.
There's no sales tax in Oregon.
He does his own taxes every April.

entries.meaning: An amount subtracted from income before tax is calculated. ---
examples: You can take a deduction for the home office.
Charitable deductions have limits.
The standard deduction went up again.

entries.meaning: Money paid back to you for something returned or overpaid. ---
examples: I'm still waiting on my tax refund.
They gave me a full refund.
No refunds after thirty days.
entries.contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (REE-fund); the verb stresses the second (ree-FUND).

entries.meaning: A general rise in prices that makes money worth less. ---
examples: Inflation ate up the raise.
Groceries went up faster than inflation.
They're trying to bring inflation down.

entries.meaning: A period when an economy shrinks and jobs disappear. ---
examples: The country slid into a recession.
He lost the house in the last recession.
Recessions hit young workers hardest.

entries.meaning: The amount by which spending exceeds income. ---
examples: The budget deficit keeps growing.
They ran a deficit three years in a row.
Trade deficits were the big story that year.

entries.meaning: The whole system of money, work and trade in a place. ---
examples: The economy added jobs last month.
Small economies depend on tourism.
The whole economy runs on credit.

entries.meaning: The management of money, especially on a large scale. ---
examples: He works in finance.
She's studying corporate finance.
Finance isn't as glamorous as people think.
entries.contrast: In the plural, finances means a person's or company's money situation.

entries.meaning: A fixed amount of money paid to an employee, usually monthly or yearly. ---
examples: She negotiated a higher salary.
Salaries here are below market.
His salary barely covers rent.

entries.meaning: The payment an employee receives for a period of work. ---
examples: They live paycheck to paycheck.
My paycheck hits on Friday.
Two paychecks came up short this month.

entries.meaning: An increase in the amount someone is paid for their work. ---
examples: I asked for a raise and got it.
Nobody's had a raise in two years.
The raises take effect in January.
entries.contrast: Americans get a raise; the British get a rise.

entries.meaning: A payment based on a percentage of what someone sells. ---
examples: Real estate agents work on commission.
He made a fat commission on that sale.
Commissions are paid at closing.

entries.meaning: Regular money paid to someone after they stop working. ---
examples: He retired on a decent pension.
The company froze its pension plan.
Pensions aren't as common as they used to be.

entries.meaning: The period of life after a person stops working for good. ---
examples: He's saving hard for retirement.
She took early retirement at fifty-eight.
Most of that money is locked up until retirement.

entries.meaning: The amount paid regularly to keep an insurance policy active. ---
examples: My premium went up after the accident.
Premiums rise every single year.
They pay the premium monthly.

entries.meaning: A written insurance contract between a company and a customer. ---
examples: He took out a life insurance policy.
Read the policy before you sign it.
Both policies expire in March.
entries.contrast: Two senses: an insurance contract, and a rule or course of action.

entries.meaning: A formal request to an insurer for money you believe you are owed. ---
examples: She filed a claim after the storm.
The insurer denied the claim.
Claims take about three weeks to process.

entries.meaning: The amount you pay yourself before insurance starts paying. ---
examples: My deductible is two thousand dollars.
A higher deductible means a lower premium.
Deductibles reset every January.

entries.meaning: Money paid regularly for the use of a home or other property. ---
examples: Rent is due on the first.
They raised the rent again.
Half my paycheck goes to rent.

entries.meaning: A person who owns property and rents it out to others. ---
examples: Our landlord finally fixed the heat.
Some landlords won't take pets.
The landlord kept the deposit.

entries.meaning: A person who pays rent to live in or use a property. ---
examples: The tenants upstairs are loud.
He's been a good tenant for six years.
The tenant gave thirty days' notice.

entries.meaning: A contract that lets someone use property for a set time in return for payment. ---
examples: Our lease is up in August.
She signed a two-year lease.
Most leases here run twelve months.

entries.meaning: An amount taken off the usual price. ---
examples: Students get a ten percent discount.
They're offering deep discounts this week.
I bought it at a discount.
entries.contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (DIS-count); the verb usually stresses the second.

entries.meaning: Something bought for much less than it is worth. ---
examples: Forty bucks for that coat is a bargain.
She hunts for bargains at estate sales.
It seemed like a bargain until it broke.

entries.meaning: A printed or digital slip that gives you money off a purchase. ---
examples: I had a coupon for a free coffee.
She clips coupons every Sunday.
The coupon expired yesterday.

entries.meaning: Something bought, or the act of buying it. ---
examples: It was an impulse purchase.
Keep receipts for all major purchases.
The purchase went through this morning.

entries.meaning: A regular payment for ongoing access to a service. ---
examples: I canceled my streaming subscription.
Subscriptions renew automatically.
The subscription runs about ten dollars a month.

entries.meaning: A statement of what a job is likely to cost. ---
examples: I got three estimates for the roof.
The estimate came in way over budget.
Their estimate didn't include labor.
entries.contrast: The noun ends in a weak ES-tuh-mut; the verb ends in a full ES-tuh-mayt.

entries.meaning: A very large amount of money. ---
examples: He made a fortune in real estate.
That dress cost a small fortune.
Family fortunes rarely last three generations.

entries.meaning: Money or property received from someone who has died. ---
examples: She spent her whole inheritance on the boat.
He's waiting on an inheritance from an aunt.
Large inheritances get taxed.

entries.meaning: The crime of getting money by deceiving people. ---
examples: He was convicted of wire fraud.
The bank flagged the charge as fraud.
Fraud costs the industry billions a year.

entries.meaning: A dishonest scheme for taking someone's money. ---
examples: It turned out to be a scam.
Phone scams target older people.
Don't fall for that scam.

entries.meaning: An official examination of financial records. ---
examples: The company is under audit.
He got hit with a tax audit.
Annual audits are required by law.

entries.meaning: The work of keeping and checking financial records. ---
examples: She majored in accounting.
Send the invoice down to accounting.
Their accounting was a mess.

entries.meaning: A person who has at least a million dollars. ---
examples: He became a millionaire overnight.
The town has more millionaires than you'd think.
She's a self-made millionaire.

entries.meaning: Someone who starts a business and takes on its financial risk. ---
examples: She's a serial entrepreneur.
The city is full of young entrepreneurs.
Every entrepreneur I know has failed at least once.
entries.contrast: French spelling, English stress — ahn-truh-pruh-NUR, with the accent on the last syllable.

entries.meaning: A person who buys goods and services for personal use. ---
examples: Consumers are spending less this year.
The law is there to protect the consumer.
Consumer prices rose again in July.

entries.meaning: A legally binding agreement between two or more parties. ---
examples: Read the contract before you sign it.
Both contracts expire in June.
They're renegotiating the contract.
entries.contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (KAHN-trakt); the verb stresses the second (kuhn-TRAKT).

entries.meaning: A maker's written promise to repair or replace a faulty product. ---
examples: The warranty covers parts and labor.
It's still under warranty.
Extended warranties are usually a bad deal.

entries.meaning: A firm promise that something will happen or be made good. ---
examples: There's no guarantee it'll work.
The store offers a money-back guarantee.
Guarantees like that aren't worth much.
entries.contrast: The u after the g is silent, and the stress lands on the last syllable.

entries.meaning: The joining of two companies into one. ---
examples: The merger fell apart at the last minute.
Regulators blocked the merger.
There have been three mergers in the industry this year.

entries.meaning: Money given for a specific purpose that does not have to be paid back. ---
examples: The lab runs on federal grants.
She won a grant to study abroad.
The grant pays for equipment only.

entries.meaning: A young company built to grow fast, usually on investors' money. ---
examples: She left the bank for a startup.
Most startups fail within five years.
The startup raised ten million dollars.

entries.meaning: The rate at which employees leave and are replaced, or the money a business takes in. ---
examples: Turnover in that department is brutal.
High turnover costs more than people think.
They cut turnover by raising starting pay.
entries.contrast: In American business English turnover usually means staff churn; the British use it for sales revenue.

entries.meaning: The state of having very little money. ---
examples: Millions of people live in poverty.
The program is aimed at reducing poverty.
He grew up in real poverty.

entries.meaning: Money or services given by an employer or the government beyond wages. ---
examples: The job comes with good benefits.
He's collecting unemployment benefits.
Health benefits start after ninety days.

entries.meaning: An amount of money given regularly for a particular purpose. ---
examples: The kids get a weekly allowance.
There's a travel allowance with the job.
Allowances haven't gone up in years.

entries.meaning: Money or goods given to help a person or organization. ---
examples: They're collecting donations for the shelter.
One anonymous donation covered the whole thing.
Your donation is tax-deductible.

entries.meaning: An organization that raises money to help people in need. ---
examples: She gives to three charities every year.
The charity runs almost entirely on volunteers.
Half the proceeds go to charity.

entries.meaning: Extra money given to someone for good service. ---
examples: Leave a decent tip.
Servers here live on tips.
The tip is already included in the total.

entries.meaning: How much something is worth in money. ---
examples: The house lost value after the flood.
Property values are climbing again.
The car's resale value is low.

entries.meaning: An amount of money. ---
examples: He owes a substantial sum.
They paid the sum in full.
Huge sums went missing from the account.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like some.

entries.meaning: Money you must pay as a penalty for breaking a rule or law.
examples: The parking fine was seventy-five dollars.
Fines double if you don't pay in thirty days.
She got a fine for the expired registration.
